items.claim: The row's own stated warrant for its close at Jer.2.37 improperly leans on the chapter division itself, which the standing rules bar as boundary evidence.
items.evidence: boundary_rationale states the close 'relies on the chapter boundary together with that shift into the divorce-law analogy, rather than on a formula of its own,' and device_notes repeats the same appeal ('the boundaries argued here from the imperative and the chapter close alone'). Chapter/verse numbering is tier-4 metadata and is never boundary evidence under the standing rules; a boundary must stand on content-based signals alone. The topic shift into the divorce-law analogy at Jer.3.1 (independently argued as an onset by the neighboring unit, and confirmed by a real addressee/discourse-imperative shift into the analogy) is adequate content-based support for the same cut point, so the proposed boundary itself is not in doubt -- the defect is evidentiary discipline, not the location of the seam.
tier_citations: standing rule: tier-4 metadata (chapter/verse numbers) is never boundary evidence

items.claim: The row's device_notes drifts into process register -- an unanchored row-count reference and an editorial-methodology statement -- rather than describing the text.
items.evidence: device_notes states 'its internal divisions in this and the following three units are cut where the bytes themselves carry a warrant, per this book's held posture on the cluster's edges.' 'The following three units' names no verse and is a bare positional/count reference rather than the verse-anchored cross-row reference the register rules require; 'this book's held posture on the cluster's edges' narrates an editorial stance on how the passage came to be divided rather than a feature of Jeremiah's own text, which is barred process/erratum register. The row's actual seam warrant is unaffected: the divorce-law analogy's topic shift at Jer.3.1 and the shuv root's earliest skeleton-tier, book-wide occurrence there (independently swept at 41 verses total, none earlier) stand on their own.
tier_citations: standing rule: cross-row references are verse-anchored; register purge bars process/editorial narration
skeleton tier: shuv root, 41 verses book-wide, earliest at Jer.3.1

items.claim: The dated 'Yahweh said to me' introduction at Jer.3.6, correctly held apart from the book's vayehi-devar-YHWH formula class, and its own verbatim repetition at Jer.3.11 jointly carry this unit's onset and close, bracketed on both sides by petuchah breaks.
items.evidence: Jer.3.6 opens with the vayomer-YHWH-elai verb plus an explicit Josiah-reign anchor, distinct from the vayehi-devar-YHWH shape used at the book's earlier word-event onsets (Jer.1.4, 1.11, 1.13, 2.1); the same verb recurs to open fresh material at Jer.3.11, correctly used as this unit's own close. Petuchah marks at Jer.3.5 and Jer.3.10 both confirm against the parashah inventory, disclosed as tier-3 weak, non-driving corroboration rather than the boundary's driver. A ketiv/qere question at Jer.3.7 was independently checked: the verse does carry a genuine ketiv/qere pair, but the row only paraphrases its content ('her treacherous sister' Judah) rather than quoting the disputed verb verbatim or cutting a boundary at that verse, so no disclosure was owed there -- unlike this same cluster's Jer.4.5 unit, which quotes its disputed word directly and discloses correctly. This confirms a heuristic false positive, not a live defect.

items.claim: The unit correctly holds the return invitation and restoration promise together as one continuing speech from Jer.3.11 through Jer.3.20, resisting an unwarranted split at the 3:19 quotation pivot.
items.evidence: The onset repeats the same speech-introduction verb as the sibling unit before it, and the close is warranted by a genuine scene shift at Jer.3.21 (narrated third-person voice replacing reported first-person divine speech). The go-and-proclaim imperative at Jer.3.12 and the renewed 'return, backsliding children' call at Jer.3.14 stay inside the single speech opened at 3:11 -- neither carries a fresh addressee, formula, or scene change of its own, so treating either as an internal cut would fragment one continuous appeal. The rejected alternative (splitting at the emphatic pivot opening Jer.3.19) is a genuine rival, correctly declined for lacking any word-event, koh-amar, or imperative marker at that point. Petuchah at Jer.3.10 and setumah at Jer.3.17 both confirm against the parashah inventory and are correctly disclosed as non-driving.

items.claim: The narrated 'a voice is heard' scene at Jer.3.21 is a genuine speaker/scene shift from the preceding first-person divine promise, and the unit's communal confession closes cleanly at Jer.3.25 ahead of Yahweh's resumed voice at Jer.4.1.
items.evidence: The shift from Yahweh's first-person promise (closing at Jer.3.20) to third-person narrated description ('a voice is heard on the bare heights') is a licensed scene-shift seam, distinct from the community's own first-person-plural confession voice that the unit then carries through to its close. Setumah at Jer.3.25 confirms against the parashah inventory as this unit's own close; the inventory is confirmed silent across Jer.3.21-3.24 and at the front seam (Jer.3.20 carries no mark), matching the row's own disclosure exactly.

items.claim: Yahweh's resumed conditional address naming Israel at Jer.4.1 is a clean speaker-and-addressee shift from the community's confession that precedes it, and the unit closes at Jer.4.2 ahead of the koh-amar onset addressed to Judah and Jerusalem at Jer.4.3.
items.evidence: The switch from the community's first-person-plural confession voice (closing at Jer.3.25) to Yahweh's own second-person conditional address naming Israel is a genuine speaker and addressee shift; the close is warranted by the fresh koh-amar formula and addressee narrowing that opens the following unit at Jer.4.3. Setumah at Jer.3.25 (shared correctly with the preceding unit's own close) and at Jer.4.2 (this unit's own close) both confirm against the parashah inventory. The shuv root's double occurrence within Jer.4.1's own conditional clause is byte-confirmed.

items.claim: The koh-amar formula at Jer.4.3, paired with the addressee's explicit narrowing to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, is the strongest-warranted seam in the cluster and correctly separates this short exhortation from the Israel-addressed oracle before it.
items.evidence: Jer.4.3 opens with ki koh amar YHWH, confirmed byte-true, and the addressee narrows explicitly from 'Israel' (Jer.4.1) to 'the men of Judah and to Jerusalem,' a combined formula-plus-addressee seam matching the licensed cut categories for this book. Setumah at Jer.4.2 confirms against the parashah inventory as the correctly-disclosed front-seam neighbor. The rejected alternative (reading Jer.4.3-4 as a continuation of the Jer.4.1-2 conditional oracle) is a genuine rival, correctly declined on the formula and addressee-narrowing grounds. High confidence is proportionate to this double warrant, and the two-verse span carries no whole-chapter cap exposure.

items.claim: The row's prose systematically substitutes pipeline 'row'/'part' vocabulary for the literary 'unit' self-reference every sibling row in this cluster uses, a register lapse repeated across all four prose fields.
items.evidence: boundary_rationale opens 'The part opens on a discourse-frame imperative pair' (a cross-part, pipeline-level self-reference) and later says the alarm sequence 'opens a fresh row rather than continuing this one'; strongest_rejected_alternative speaks of not splitting Jer.4.7 'into its own row'; device_notes says a mark 'does not drive this row's boundary' and refers twice more to 'the row's own imperative' / 'the row's Hebrew splice.' Every other row in this cluster uses 'unit'/'span' exclusively for the same kind of self-reference and never uses 'row,' so this is a genuine, repeated deviation rather than incidental wording. The underlying boundary claim is unaffected: the discourse-imperative alarm cluster opening at Jer.4.5 (with its ketiv/qere correctly disclosed against the pointed qere actually quoted) runs to a close at Jer.4.9 where neum-YHWH is correctly used as closure corroboration only, ahead of the prophet's own first-person onset at Jer.4.10.
tier_citations: standing rule: register purge -- self-reference is 'this unit,' not 'this row'; cross-part references barred
